disclaimer: This report is for educational and wellness purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace advice from a qualified healthcare professional. HbA1c results should be confirmed by your doctor. Do not start, stop or change any medication without medical advice.

status.label: In the diabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is 6.5% or above, the range used to diagnose diabetes. A single result is not a diagnosis: your doctor will confirm it with a repeat test or another blood test.
status.urgent_message: Your HbA1c is 10% or higher. Please contact a doctor soon — within the next few days — rather than waiting for a routine appointment. Seek urgent care if you have extreme thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, confusion or vomiting.

summary: Because your HbA1c of 11.2% is in the diabetes range and quite high, it's important to contact a doctor soon rather than wait. Your results also show a BMI in the obese range, kidney disease, low activity, and age-related risk, all of which add to your overall health risk and work together with blood sugar levels. The most valuable next steps are getting your kidney function, blood pressure, and cardiovascular risk checked promptly, following your calorie target and protein/potassium guidance closely, and building gentle regular activity into your routine. Working closely with your care team now can help you manage these risk factors over time.

comorbidity_assessment.note: High blood sugar can put extra strain on the kidneys over time, and kidney function also affects how the body handles protein, potassium, and phosphorus, so these need close monitoring together.
Carrying extra weight can make it harder for the body to use insulin effectively, which is why gradual, steady weight loss is often a helpful part of overall care.

constraints: Do not follow high-protein diets or take protein supplements; keep protein moderate unless your kidney doctor advises otherwise.
Do not use potassium-based salt substitutes; ask your doctor whether you need to limit potassium or phosphorus.
Follow the calorie target; avoid sugary drinks and fruit juices completely.
Fill half the plate with non-starchy vegetables to stay full on fewer calories.

foods_to_eat: Non-starchy vegetables such as broccoli, spinach, zucchini, and peppers
Whole grains like barley, quinoa, and oats in moderate portions
Lean proteins such as skinless chicken, turkey, fish, and tofu in modest amounts
Healthy fats like olive oil, avocado, and a small handful of nuts
Low-sodium herbs and spices such as garlic, basil, oregano, and lemon juice for flavor
foods_to_avoid: Sugary drinks, sodas, and fruit juices
Refined flour products like white bread and pastries
Excess red meat and processed meats
plan.portion_guidance: Fill half your plate with non-starchy vegetables, one quarter with a modest portion of lean protein (about the size of a deck of cards), and one quarter with whole grains or starchy vegetables. Keep protein portions moderate given your kidney health, and avoid large servings of meat or protein supplements.
plan.hydration: Drink water throughout the day as your main beverage. Avoid sugary drinks and fruit juices entirely. If you have been told to watch your fluid or potassium intake, follow your doctor's specific guidance on how much to drink each day.
based_on: kidney disease: moderate protein, no potassium substitutes
obesity: emphasis on non-starchy vegetables and portion control

exercise: Start with gentle, low-impact activities such as short walks or seated exercises, since you're currently sedentary and have kidney disease and joint protection needs.
Build up slowly toward 150 minutes a week of moderate activity, adding a few minutes every week rather than jumping to a high level right away.
Include light muscle-strengthening activities (such as resistance bands or bodyweight exercises) on 2 days a week, keeping movements gentle to protect your joints.
Avoid high-impact or jarring movements that stress the joints; choose activities like swimming, stationary cycling, or walking on soft surfaces.
lifestyle.walking_goal: Begin with about 10 minutes of walking, 5 days a week, and gradually build up to 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week, as your comfort and stamina improve.
lifestyle.weight_management: Since your BMI is in the obese range, a gradual weight loss of about 5–10% of your current body weight over the next 6 months is a reasonable and safe goal. Focus on steady, sustainable changes rather than quick fixes, and check in regularly with your healthcare provider given your kidney condition to make sure your plan stays safe for you.
lifestyle.sleep: Aim for 7 to 9 hours of sleep each night. Try to keep a consistent bedtime and wake time, limit screens for an hour before bed, keep your bedroom cool and dark, and avoid caffeine in the afternoon and evening.
stress: Practice slow, deep breathing for a few minutes each day, especially during stressful moments, to help calm your body's stress response.
Try a short daily mindfulness or relaxation practice, such as guided meditation or gentle stretching, to help manage day-to-day stress.
Consider keeping a simple journal to note stressful triggers and how you respond to them, which can help you build healthier coping habits over time.
behaviour_change: Since you're a former smoker, staying smoke-free is a great achievement for your health — if you ever feel at risk of relapse, support services like quitlines or your doctor can help you stay on track.
Avoid regular use of painkillers such as ibuprofen without medical advice, since these can affect kidney health.
Set small, specific goals each week (like adding 5 minutes to your walk) to build sustainable habits gradually.
Keep regular follow-ups with your healthcare team to monitor your kidney health and overall progress.

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Shows your average blood glucose over about 3 months and whether your plan is working.
monitoring.frequency: Every 3 months until your doctor says you are at target, then every 6 months

monitoring.name: Kidney function (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
monitoring.why: High glucose and blood pressure can quietly damage the kidneys; these tests find it early.
monitoring.frequency: Every year, or more often if you already have kidney disease

monitoring.name: Dilated eye examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can damage the retina (diabetic retinopathy) long before your vision changes.
monitoring.frequency: Soon after diabetes is confirmed, then every year (your eye doctor may extend this to every 2 years if exams stay clear)

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

monitoring.name: Cardiovascular risk assessment
monitoring.why: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in people with diabetes.

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

monitoring.name: Post-meal (post-prandial) blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows how your body handles glucose after meals, which HbA1c alone can hide.

monitoring.name: Lipid profile (cholesterol)
monitoring.why: Diabetes and high cholesterol together raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
monitoring.frequency: Every year (at least every 5 years if you are under 40), or as your doctor advises
risk_indicators: Existing cholesterol problem or heart disease

monitoring.name: Liver check (liver tests and FIB-4 score)
monitoring.why: Fatty liver is common with diabetes and obesity and can progress without symptoms.
monitoring.frequency: FIB-4 score every 1–2 years, or sooner if your doctor finds a higher risk

monitoring.name: Vitamin B12
monitoring.why: Metformin, a common diabetes medicine, can lower B12 over time; low B12 can mimic nerve damage.
monitoring.frequency: Ask your doctor, especially if you take metformin (often checked yearly)
risk_indicators: Vegetarian or vegan diet (lower dietary B12)

monitoring.name: Vitamin D
monitoring.why: Low vitamin D is more common with obesity and kidney disease; testing is not routine for everyone.
monitoring.frequency: Only if your doctor recommends it

monitoring.name: Foot examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can reduce feeling and blood flow in the feet, so small injuries go unnoticed.
monitoring.frequency: A full exam every year; check your own feet daily

preventive_actions: Schedule kidney function tests (eGFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio) and blood pressure checks soon given these are highlighted priorities.
Keep protein moderate and avoid potassium-based salt substitutes until your kidney doctor gives specific guidance.
Follow your 1600 calorie target, filling half your plate with non-starchy vegetables and avoiding sugary drinks.
Start physical activity gently, building up slowly to protect your joints and support gradual weight loss.
Book a dilated eye exam and cardiovascular risk assessment, since both are flagged as priority checks.
Avoid regular use of painkillers like ibuprofen without checking with your doctor first, since these can affect kidney health.

hba1c_caveat: HbA1c can be less accurate if you have anaemia, kidney disease, a recent blood transfusion or certain haemoglobin variants.
